Hatchlings of the Stubby Bobtail (Rossia pacifica) emerge from their egg capsules after an embryonic period of one hundred and fifty days [ab = one hundred and fifty days] when reared at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these neonates possess a mantle length of just half a centimeter (0.5 centimeter) [Lb = 0.5 centimeter] and a corresponding wet weight of only one-tenth of a gram (0.1 gram) [Wwb = 0.1 gram]. This diminutive size at birth is typical of many cephalopods that produce large numbers of small offspring, though it contrasts with some deeper-water relatives that lay fewer, larger eggs. The prolonged incubation period at this relatively low temperature reflects the metabolic constraints typical of cold-water marine invertebrates, where developmental rates are tightly coupled to ambient thermal conditions. Upon emerging from the protective gelatinous capsule, the hatchlings are immediately capable of active swimming and begin a planktonic existence, preying on small crustaceans.

As the juvenile Stubby Bobtail grows, it undergoes a period of rapid somatic development that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], individuals reach puberty at approximately 244 days since birth [tp = approximately 244 days since birth]. This marked delay before reproductive competence is a common feature among sepiolid squids, allowing sufficient time for the accumulation of somatic mass and the maturation of reproductive organs. During this pre-pubertal phase, the mantle grows steadily, and the animal transitions from a purely planktonic diet to one that includes small benthic shrimp and amphipods. The onset of gonadal activity is signaled by behavioral changes, including an increased tendency to bury in soft sediments during daylight hours. This relatively protracted juvenile period, spanning many months at this temperature, suggests that Rossia pacifica follows a moderately slow life-history pace compared to more tropical cephalopod species.

Throughout the reproductive lifespan of the Stubby Bobtail, females accrue a total cumulative reproductive output of fifty eggs  when maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This lifetime fecundity is partitioned across multiple successive spawning events, with each clutch typically containing a modest number of eggs that are deposited singly upon the substrate. The energetic investment per egg is considerable relative to the female's body mass, as each capsule is provisioned with ample yolk to support the long embryonic development period. Field observations suggest that females may allocate a substantial fraction of their somatic reserves to egg production over the course of their adult lives, a strategy consistent with a single, terminal spawning event typical of many coleoid cephalopods. At the conclusion of the breeding period, the female's body condition deteriorates markedly as she has exhausted her stored resources, leading inevitably to senescence.

The final mantle length attained by Rossia pacifica at the time of death has been recorded at approximately 3.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 3.5 centimeters], a value that represents the culmination of months of continuous somatic growth. This terminal size is modest compared to many other cephalopods but is typical of small benthic sepiolids that occupy the continental shelf. The complete lifespan of individuals reared under stable conditions at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] spans approximately 579.5 days [am = approximately 579.5 days], encompassing the embryonic period, the extended juvenile phase, and the relatively brief reproductive window. Such a lifespan, lasting nearly nineteen months, is consistent with a semelparous life-history strategy in which a single, intense reproductive effort precedes physiological death. The post-reproductive decline is characterized by a cessation of feeding, progressive loss of body condition, and cessation of locomotory activity, culminating in natural mortality.

In comparative context, the life-history strategy of the Stubby Bobtail aligns well with other cold-water sepiolids that exhibit slow growth and delayed reproduction. The pre-pubertal phase of roughly eight months [tp = roughly eight months] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is a period during which the animal accumulates sufficient somatic reserves to support the subsequent reproductive effort. This prolonged maturation interval is thought to reflect the metabolic constraints imposed by the chronically low temperatures of the species' Northeast Pacific habitat, where metabolic rates are suppressed and growth consequently proceeds at a reduced pace.
